public_rationale: The evidence supports variable success and substantial limits on advance prediction. It does not establish that users can never identify successful substitutions beforehand. Earlier research also shows that advance confidence can contain useful information, although it transfers imperfectly to unfamiliar tasks. These findings do not settle whether a method meets the ordinary standard of dependable advance identification across the work Marcus discusses. Scoring the whole claim as supported would turn limited experiments into a universal conclusion; scoring it as contradicted would treat partial predictability as sufficient without establishing that it is dependable.
limitations: The principal evaluation uses question-answering benchmarks rather than complete human workflows.
The observation period and meaning of dependable identification require interpretation.
The accessible studies do not exhaust possible prediction methods.

our_interpretation: The claim concerns practical substitution for human task performance, not whether LLMs have human cognition.

The plain reading is that users cannot dependably distinguish successful from unsuccessful substitutions before the particular attempt. This does not require philosophical certainty, but a weak predictive association is insufficient to contradict it.

The observation concerns capabilities at publication. With no specified reporting interval for research results, I use the current reporting year, 2025, restricted to findings available by August 12. Earlier studies provide context.
A task succeeds when it meets independently specified requirements. Answer checking after execution does not count as advance prediction.
criteria.support_condition: Evaluations show both successful and unsuccessful task performance. Supporting the additional categorical claim requires evidence that dependable advance identification is unavailable across the claimed scope; failure of a few prediction methods alone is insufficient.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A method validated on previously unseen cases dependably identifies successful or unsuccessful substitutions before execution within a clearly defined task class. Merely predicting average performance, or checking completed answers, is insufficient.

evidence.explanation: PredictaBoard measures successes and failures and tests predictors that operate before the subject LLM receives an input. Its tested predictors leave almost no usable region above the discussed 95% accuracy threshold, supporting limited predictability in this setting without establishing universal impossibility.

evidence.excerpt: Models perform well at predicting P(IK) and partially generalize across tasks, though they struggle with calibration of P(IK) on new tasks.
evidence.explanation: The study predicts whether a model knows an answer without inspecting a proposed answer, showing that advance information is possible. It predates the target period and does not establish dependable prediction of human-task substitution across unfamiliar settings.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A verified prospective study of models available at publication, using representative substitution tasks, predefined success requirements, and reported prediction errors and coverage, could establish a dependable counterexample. Supporting the categorical impossibility would require substantially broader evidence than failures of particular methods.
